rv.q: What could have been an acting stunt is instead a rich, deep portrait of a woman who, somehow, is deeply revealed without giving much of her mysterious self away.
Mirren, who is becoming something of an expert on playing English royalty, creates an astonishing portrayal, by turns prickly and chummy, regal and regular, insecure and temperamental.
Helen Mirren is absolutely terrific as Queen Elizabeth II in 'The Audience.'
But it’s Mirren's comic timing that sets the performance apart.
At moments like this, we are all the adoring subjects of this Queen.
Whether you know your 20th-century Parliamentary history or simply get an Anglophile high from tea service and footmen in livery, Mirren rules in this engaging and humanizing retrospective.
Indeed, its most memorable moment might well be when Mirren transforms into a much younger version of the monarch, as the play sweeps back in time right before our eyes.
While not a brilliant play, The Audience illuminates the reassuring continuity that has made the Monarchy so beloved in the U.K.
Mirren is, of course, excellent.
The play might be a fragmented portrait, but it’s nonetheless a full-bodied one, in which Mirren does a graceful jete across the years from the savvy diplomatic novice to the shrewd veteran observer.
Those transformations, accomplished with sleights of hand worthy of a master magician, are probably the most entertaining and satisfying aspects of “The Audience.”
But even aside from its authenticity issues, The Audience relies on too many clichés of biodrama to hold itself together.
Some of the meetings may not be exactly scintillating, but they make you consider the grace with which Queen Elizabeth has endured the passing parade.
This is Mirren's show, and she fully lives up to the expectation created by the buzz from her Olivier Award-winning turn in the West End production of the play in 2013.
But if you came to see royalty—acting royalty, that is—this is an Audience worth seeking.
She’s given performance one for the ages.

Of course it's Helen Mirren's brilliant portrayal of Elizabeth II from age twenty-five to her eighties makes you hail this monarch and all the Prime Ministers with whom she has weekly briefing meetings or audiences.
But taken as a whole, “The Audience” is a fascinating meditation on the historic and present day role of the English monarch.
Those of you who like a bit of Royal Fantasy should hurry up and get your tickets to this delicious bit of sweets
An audience with Helen Mirren makes a fine night's entertainment, but not--in this case--a compelling dramatic event.
The Broadway star vehicle she's driving lacks the high-octane fuel to take her there, even though it's stylishly directed by Stephen Daldry and eloquently designed by Bob Crowley.
“The Audience” makes the best case ever for ridding the United Kingdom of the royal family.

That’s all very well, but it is Mirren’s magnificent performance as Elizabeth that makes “The Audience” such a must-see show for anyone interested in modern British history or simply the woman upon the throne.
'The Audience' is spectacular and a must watch.
But Morgan's play is foremost a fascinating character study, brought to life by Mirren's stunning performance as the Queen.
Mirren is mesmerizing as she plays Queen Elizabeth
While she has no grandstanding scenes, Mirren’s natural authority and the subtlety with which she offers nuance upon nuance to her performance make seeing her a must.
We have a feeling Mirren will also hear shouts of “Best Actress” coming as Drama Desk, Outer Critics and Tony Awards nominations are announced.
Certainly, there will be less familiarity with some of the memory-jogging details seeded into the dialogue.

Other than the chance to see Ms. Mirren onstage or to witness some conjectural conversations between Queen Elizabeth II and her numerous prime ministers over her long reign, there's really not a lot of reason to see The Audience.
